claims.reason: Passage 6 states that AI's fundamental instinct is to please humans, albeit somewhat inaccurately.
Passage 7 explicitly says the problems AI needs to solve can be split into two distinct categories.
Passage 8 describes the first category as problems with standard answers (e.g., mathematics) having a single correct path and verifiable through multiple pathways.
Passage 9 defines the second category as problems with no standard answers, judged by human intent, creating a gray zone especially difficult in the humanities.
Passage 10 states that the more standardized a text is, the better AI performs, citing highly constrained documents with standardized formats.
Passage 11 directly states that the more a text requires deep thinking and genuine creation, the more unreliable AI becomes.
Passage 15 observes that AI exhibits excitement and creativity when discussing abstract, semi-philosophical topics with no standard answer, but cannot yield definitive conclusions.
Passage 17 identifies high-level control of long-form text as another major hurdle.
Passage 19 proposes making AI write actual prose while simultaneously composing and refining the subsequent plot outline.
Passage 20 describes the challenge of transforming AI using skeletons to anchor wild ideas into cohesive works.
Passage 22 speculates that if the pipeline proves viable, AI could create non-detective novels exceeding one million words that remain highly readable.
Passage 24 states that all reflections aim to treat and use AI as an ordinary person possessing the inherent advantages and structural flaws of human cognitive patterns.

omitted_concepts.description: AI as a state machine filtered during training to satisfy humans; failures are denied release.
Standard-answer problems allow multi-path verification ('all roads lead to Rome').
The 'thousand Hamlets' dilemma and scarcity of universally acclaimed masterpieces in humanities.
Human writers are also unreliable; gap between wild conception and poor execution.
Two core novel frameworks: non-fiction plot and construction (e.g., golden first three chapters, American TV tropes).
AI's abstract creativity can be leveraged specifically for creating attractive characters.
Writers often draft outline while writing; inspiration as cumulative time × cognitive efficiency.
High probability of failure; even partial success maps outer limits of AI in humanities.

review.summary: All 12 claims are faithful paraphrases of their cited passages. The extraction covers the article's core arguments: AI's human-pleasing instinct, the two problem categories, text standardization effects, AI's abstract creativity, long-form control hurdle, the proposed simultaneous writing/outlining method, the skeleton-anchoring principle, the million-word viability forecast, and the overarching human-cognition framing. No claims are unsupported, duplicated, or misattributed. Omitted concepts include the state-machine training filter, multi-path verification, the Hamlets dilemma, human unreliability, novel construction frameworks, character-creation leverage, the simultaneous drafting workflow, and the high failure probability.
